newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis seen dragging on for months.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis seen dragging on for months.

text.p: With few signs of progress in negotiations, most Peruvians now believe it may be months before 72 hostages held by Marxist rebels at the Japanese ambassador's house are freed, an opinion poll showed on Sunday.

Sixty-two percent of respondents told Apoyo pollsters they thought the nearly four-months-old siege could go on for another one to three months or even more, Peru's Panamericana television network reported.
Only 15 percent of those questioned during April 4-7 thought the siege by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels could end in less than one month.

The survey of 512 people also revealed most Peruvians still favoured a negotiated solution, with seven out of 10 saying they supported a continuation of the talks and the rest proposing sending troops in.

Hours before the poll results were released, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, part of a three-man panel overseeing talks between the rebels and government, visited the residence to hold Mass for the hostages. He said negotiations to end the 117-day siege were creeping forward.

"The talks go on advancing," he told reporters before entering the compound, presumably also for fresh talks with MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa. "We are in a stage of (giving out) very little information. We must not give out any information."

Outside the Japanese residence, police cordoning off the area donned black T-shirts bearing a "Rescue of the Hostages" slogan and a picture of four officers descending on ropes from an airborne helicopter.

While Cipriani delivered spiritual support to the men, only a few blocks away their relatives attended a special Mass. "We have come to pray close to them. We are so close to them and yet so far," said Beatriz de Gumucio, wife of captive Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio.

Police believe that rebel leader Cerpa wants to end the siege peacefully, according to a three-page report obtained by Reuters based on an analysis of handwritten notes found in the Japanese residence's garbage.
"He probably wants to be remembered as a hero that achieved his goals without bloodshed," the report said.

Sources close to the talks say negotiations are zeroing in on the rebels' demand of freedom for jailed comrades in exchange for their captives. President Alberto Fujimori has publicly ruled out releasing any MRTA prisoners, but sources there was room for possible sentence reductions for low-ranking MRTA prisoners or release of those detained but not convicted.
Sunday's opinion poll, which gave no margin of error, showed seven out of 10 Peruvians were against releasing even those MRTA inmates jailed for minor offences.

About 20 MRTA rebels swept into the Japanese mansion during a cocktail party on Dec. 17 and took all 500 guests hostage. They gradually released all but 72 of them, keeping two Cabinet ministers, Fujimori's brother and top Japanese businessmen.
